extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing stand-up material focused on three linked techniques: the rule-of-three, callbacks, and comedic anachronisms. Includes definitions, examples, and practice/homework suggestions for using these devices in a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-of-three (establish, reinforce, surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic rule-of-three: establish, reinforce, surprise. The first two items create a pattern (set-up) and the third subverts it (payoff). Two items cannot establish a pattern that the third can disrupt; three is the minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Example formulation: “Monday, Tuesday, Banana.” First two establish expectation, third is the gag. Tony Allen’s definition: ‘establish, reinforce, surprise.’ Use three items where the third takes the idea to an extreme or unexpected place. Avoid unnecessarily long lists — comedy is economical and you don’t need to stretch the pattern (e.g., “Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Banana” is wasteful). Homework: when you have a list in material, make it three in length and make the third a curveball. Thousands of examples exist (e.g., Bill Bailey’s “mini bar, trouser press, baby Jesus in a bidet”).

(Scoring/quality notes implied: clarity of pattern in the first two and strength/originality of the surprise in the third determine effectiveness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice and punch for the payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing the right word for the payoff is crucial — certain words have more comedic ‘punch’ and will land the gag better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by switching ‘banana’ to ‘Norway’ (still makes the structural point but loses laughs). Consider syllable, consonant sounds (e.g., belief that the ‘k’ sound is funny), rhythm, and unexpectedness. Test variants: subtle changes can turn an audible chuckle into nothing. Try options like ‘trousers,’ ‘knickers,’ etc., and prefer words that give the punch necessary for the payoff. (Anti-pattern: using an accurate but bland word that removes comic surprise.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and concision in joke construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should be economical: don’t use more elements than necessary to establish a pattern or make a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Two items aren’t enough to set a pattern for a subversion; three is ideal and adding more items dilutes the gag. Example anti-pattern: listing four items then throwing in a gag item (e.g., Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Banana) loses punch. Use just enough detail to set expectations and get to the payoff quickly.

(Practical note: keep setups short so callbacks and payoffs register clearly later in the set.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Callback (reintroducing earlier material)
rubrics_metrics.description: A callback is bringing something from earlier in the set back in a new context, often unexpectedly. It’s a well-known device and frequently used as an ending; it reliably gets a laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bill Bailey’s donkey cocaine setup (donkey snorting cocaine) later returns as the ‘donkey with the nosebleed’ when directions are given. Callbacks can be woven through a set (Harry Hill’s web of callbacks) and can function as a structural device or punchline. When assembling a set, identify earlier references you can reintroduce in a new, surprising context. Homework example: mention expensive socks early, then later reveal you need a pay rise to support your sock habit. You can also call back to things other comics have said or to incidents that happened earlier in the room during a club gig. (Quality: effective callbacks feel inevitable yet surprising; over-explaining or forcing callbacks weakens them.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anachronism (modern details in historical settings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anachronistic comedy inserts modern-day details, attitudes, or information into a historical setting; it can be presented as a ‘what if’ or as if it’s accurate, and it’s a staple technique for history-set comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples: Bill Bailey’s nativity with a ‘mini bar, trouser press, baby Jesus in a bidet’; Eddie Izzard wishing Romans would hurry to get straight roads. Technique: pick a historical period and inject modern conveniences, slang, or attitudes to create incongruity. The comic effect may come from playing it straight (as if accurate) or from obvious absurdity (‘what if’ scenarios). Homework: choose a period you want to talk about and bring in modern details — part of the fun is committing to the premise.

(Performance note: anachronisms work best when the audience recognizes the historical baseline and the modern insertion disrupts expectations.)
